title: B2 capstone: argument and nuance
objectives: I can explain why each word in this unit is written and stressed as it is, using the stress rule, the accent marks and the letter-to-sound rules.
I can choose the indicative, subjunctive, conditional or personal infinitive by asking whether the speaker is asserting the clause and which time slot it belongs to.

I can argue a position with nuance using concessive and adversative structures such as por mais que, ainda que, mesmo assim and apesar disso, and explain why some take the subjunctive and others do not.
I can switch between informal and formal registers depending on the situation.
I can emphasize a word with foi... que, é que, quem... é and o que... é, and avoid common errors made by advanced learners.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on the third to last syllable, so the accent is always written, and an open e takes the acute. T before the sound i is ch, so the word is said E-chi-ka. The adjective is ético, and the plural is éticas, as in questões éticas.

example.target: A ética é importante nas decisões das empresas.
example.source: Ethics is important in companies' decisions.

vocabulary.note: Abstract nouns in -idade (English -ity) are stressed on da, the second to last syllable, which is exactly what the final e predicts, so they never need an accent. T before i is ch and the d before the weak final e is j: i-dẽ-chi-DA-ji.

example.target: A língua faz parte da identidade de um povo.
example.source: Language is part of a people's identity.
example.source_literal: The language makes part of-the identity of a people.

vocabulary.note: Built from des- (not), igual (equal) and -dade (-ity). The gu before a keeps the u: it is said w. L at the end of a syllable is also w, and s between vowels is z, so the word is said de-zi-gwaw-DA-ji. It is stressed on da, so no accent is written.

example.target: A desigualdade social é um dos maiores desafios do país.
example.source: Social inequality is one of the country's biggest challenges.

vocabulary.note: From sustentar (to hold up), the ending -ável (able to be) and -idade (-ity). The ending -ável becomes -abil- before -idade. Because it ends in -dade it is stressed on da and needs no accent: sus-tẽ-ta-bi-li-DA-ji.

example.target: A sustentabilidade exige mudanças em toda a cadeia de produção.
example.source: Sustainability requires changes throughout the production chain.
example.source_literal: The sustainability demands changes in all the chain of production.

vocabulary.note: The adjective follows the noun, as usual. Inteligência is stressed on gên, the third to last syllable (cia counts as two vowels), so the accent is required; the e is closed and sits before n, so it is the circumflex. G before e is zh and c before i is s. Artificial ends in l, so it is stressed on the last syllable and needs no accent: ar-chi-fi-SYAW.

example.target: A inteligência artificial já está presente em muitos serviços.
example.source: Artificial intelligence is already present in many services.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on the third to last syllable, so the accent is required, and the closed e before m takes the circumflex: po-LÊ-mi-ca. The adjective is polêmico, meaning controversial.

example.target: A decisão gerou uma grande polêmica nas redes sociais.
example.source: The decision caused a big controversy on social media.
example.source_literal: The decision generated a big controversy in-the networks social.

vocabulary.note: Takes de: discordo de você, discordo dessa ideia. The opposite is concordar com. D before the sound i is j, so the first syllable is jis; the s before c is s or sh depending on the region.

example.target: Respeito sua opinião, mas discordo dela.

example.source_literal: I-respect your opinion, but I-disagree of-it.

vocabulary.source: to weigh up, to consider carefully
vocabulary.note: From Latin pondus, weight, the same root as English ponder. It is used for weighing ideas, not objects (for objects use pesar). The on is a nasal vowel, and the ending r makes the last syllable the stressed one: põ-de-RAR.

example.target: É preciso ponderar os riscos antes de decidir.
example.source: The risks must be weighed before deciding.
example.source_literal: Is necessary to-weigh the risks before of to-decide.

vocabulary.note: In the sense of arguing a position it is followed by que and the indicative, because the speaker reports an assertion: ela sustenta que o problema é estrutural. It also means to support physically or financially, which is its literal sense.

example.target: Ela sustenta que o problema é estrutural.
example.source: She maintains that the problem is structural.

vocabulary.note: R at the start of a word is the strong r, the breathy h of English hat: he-fu-TAR. The ending r makes the last syllable the stressed one, so no accent is written.

example.target: O pesquisador refutou os argumentos com dados concretos.
example.source: The researcher refuted the arguments with concrete data.

vocabulary.note: A fixed phrase. Conta is an account or a bill, and levar is to carry. The em is a nasal vowel, said ẽy.

example.target: Precisamos levar em conta a opinião dos moradores.
example.source: We need to take the residents' opinion into account.
example.source_literal: We-need to-carry in account the opinion of-the residents.

vocabulary.source: on the other hand, in return
vocabulary.note: Introduces something which balances the previous point, often an advantage set against a cost, like a counterweight. A plain contrast is mas or por outro lado. T before the sound i is ch: kõ-tra-par-CHI-da.

example.target: O projeto é caro; em contrapartida, traz benefícios duradouros.
example.source: The project is expensive; on the other hand, it brings lasting benefits.
example.source_literal: The project is expensive; in counterpart, it-brings benefits lasting.

vocabulary.note: Always followed by the subjunctive. It concedes any degree, and it can also be built around an adjective: por mais difícil que seja. Mais is said with the diphthong ai, which is why it is not mas.

example.target: Por mais que eu tente, não consigo entender.
example.source: No matter how hard I try, I cannot understand.
example.source_literal: For more that I try, not I-manage to-understand.

vocabulary.note: Always followed by the subjunctive. Ainda is said a-Ĩ-da: the n makes the i nasal, so ai is two beats here, not the diphthong of pai.

example.target: Ainda que seja difícil, vale a pena tentar.
example.source: Even though it is difficult, it is worth trying.
example.source_literal: Still that be difficult, is-worth the pain to-try.

vocabulary.note: Starts a new main clause and takes the indicative. Mesmo is said MEZ-mu, because s before the voiced consonant m is z. Assim ends in the nasal im: a-SĨ, and ss between vowels is s.

example.target: Estava cansado; mesmo assim, foi ao treino.
example.source: He was tired; even so, he went to practice.
example.source_literal: He-was tired; same thus, he-went to-the training.

vocabulary.note: Disso is de plus isso: apesar de needs a noun or an infinitive, and isso is the pronoun that stands for the whole previous statement. Apesar is said a-pe-ZAR, with s between vowels as z, and ss in disso is s.

example.target: Choveu muito; apesar disso, o evento aconteceu.
example.source: It rained a lot; despite that, the event took place.
example.source_literal: It-rained much; in-spite of-that, the event happened.

vocabulary.note: Fundo is the bottom or the depth, said FŨ-du with a nasal vowel. The phrase points to what is true beneath the surface. Fundo also means fund, as in fundo de requalificação in the first dialogue.

vocabulary.note: Ver is the infinitive used as a noun, so the phrase says 'at my seeing'. It softens an opinion and is slightly formal. Variants: na minha opinião, do meu ponto de vista.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: accents and stress in the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
This note applies the method from the stress lesson to the new words of this unit, so that no accent is left unexplained. The method never changes. Divide the word into syllables, find the stressed syllable by ear, read the default from the ending, and compare. If the stress agrees with the default, nothing is written. If it disagrees, the stressed vowel carries a mark: the acute if the vowel is open, the circumflex if it is closed. An accent is therefore never decoration. It says that this word breaks the default of its ending, and it shows which vowel is stressed.

Most accents in this unit sit in the vocabulary of ideas, which comes from Latin and Greek and falls into a few large families. The first family is the proparoxytones, the words stressed on the third to last syllable: ética, décadas, crédito, público, básico. No ending predicts that stress, so the accent is always written. A final ia, io or ua counts as two vowels for this purpose, so inteligência, notícia, privilégio, princípios, funcionários and necessárias all belong here. Compare tia, where the stressed vowel is the i itself and nothing is written. The second family is the adjectives in -vel, which means able to be: inevitável, possível, sustentável, reutilizável. A word ending in l is stressed on the last syllable by default, but these are stressed one syllable earlier, so the accent is always written, and it stays in the plural (possíveis, inacessíveis). The third family is a case where the ending lets you skip the accent. The abstract nouns in -idade (identidade, desigualdade, sustentabilidade, responsabilidade) are stressed on da, the second to last syllable, which is exactly what the final e predicts, so they need no mark however long they are.

The choice between acute and circumflex follows the quality of the vowel. In polêmica and inteligência the stressed e is closed and sits before an m or n, where Brazilian spelling writes the circumflex in the middle of a word, as in câmera and acadêmico. In ética, crédito and privilégio the stressed e is open, so the mark is the acute. The vowels i and u have only one quality, so they take only the acute (público, dúvida).

The second group of accents belongs to words stressed on the last syllable. A word with that stress needs a mark when it ends in a, e, o, em or es, because those endings predict the second to last syllable: você, Canadá, será, terá, até, também, porém, viés. A stressed one-syllable word ending in a, e or o, with or without a final s, takes a mark too: já, lá, é, nós, três. The informal spoken forms are built in exactly this way. Cê is você with its first syllable dropped, tá is está, tô is estou and né is não é. Each is a stressed one-syllable word, so each is written with its accent even though the spelling records casual speech.

The default is recomputed every time a word takes a new ending, so an accent can appear or vanish. Viés is vi-ÉS, stressed on the last syllable, where the ending es predicts the second to last, so it has the acute. Its plural vieses is vi-É-zes, stressed on the second to last syllable, which es does predict, so the mark is no longer needed. The plural -veis of the -vel adjectives behaves the other way: it still predicts the last syllable, so the accent stays.

Four more marks have other jobs. The tilde makes a vowel nasal and, when no other accent is written, also marks the stress, so produção, decisão, formação, educação, são, estão and surgirão need nothing more: the ending ão predicts the last syllable, and that is where the stress is. The same holds for the plural -ões (decisões, revoluções), the ending õe (propõe) and mãe. The hiatus accent keeps a stressed i or u from merging with the neighboring vowel into a diphthong: país is pa-ÍS in two beats and saúde is sa-Ú-de. The circumflex in têm is a differential accent, which only distinguishes the plural from the singular in writing because both are said the same way: ele tem, eles têm. Finally the grave accent in às is crase: in sirva às pessoas, the preposition a (servir a, to serve) fuses with the article as, and the grave records the fusion, as ao does with a masculine word.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: letters and sound patterns in this unit
grammar.explanation:
The reading procedure from the sounds lesson works on every new word: look for marks, group the letters that work as a unit, apply the rules to the remaining letters, weaken the final vowels and place the stress. This note runs that procedure on the recurring patterns of the words in this unit. Most of it is four rules that you already know. First, t and d change to ch and j before the sound i, and the weak final e counts as that sound, so ética is E-chi-ka and identidade ends in da-ji. Second, l at the end of a syllable is said w, which turns desigualdade into de-zi-gwaw-DA-ji and julgamento into zhuw-ga-MẼ-tu. Third, m or n after a vowel and before a consonant is not a consonant at all: it marks the vowel as nasal (fundo, inteligência, sustentar, empresas). Fourth, a single s between vowels is z and ss is s, so apesar is said with z and disso with s.

Some letters work in pairs. Qu and gu before e or i keep the hard sound and the u is silent (que, quem, pesquisador, pouquinho); before a or o the u is pronounced as w (quando, requalificação, desigualdade). A few words are exceptions that must be learned, such as frequência and aguentar, where the u is said before e. Ch is sh (chega, choveu), lh is the ly of million (trabalhadores, melhor) and nh is the ny of canyon (senhor, senhora); the h of these three never sounds on its own. Rr between two vowels is the strong r, the breathy h of English hat, and so is a word-initial r (garrafa, carreira, erra, refutar). A single r between vowels is a quick tap, like the tt of American butter (garantir, prefeitura).

The soft and hard sounds of c and g follow the next letter. Before e or i, c is s (aconteceu, funcionários) and g is zh (inteligência, exige, surgirão, corrigir); before a, o or u, c is k and g is hard (garantir, julgamento). The letter j is always zh, and h is always silent (humano, hábitos). The cedilla writes the s sound before a, o or u: mudanças, educação, serviços, desapareçam. The letter x has no single rule, but one pattern is useful here: in the prefix ex before a vowel it is z, so exige is e-ZI-zhi. Between vowels there is no rule: lixo in the dialogue is simply learned as LI-shu.

On vowels, remember that two strong vowels side by side are two beats, never a diphthong, which is why surpreendeu is sur-pre-en-DEU, with ee as two beats followed by the diphthong eu, and saneamento is sa-ne-a-MẼ-tu. The diphthongs in this unit are ei (treino, cadeia), eu (choveu), ou (transformou, pouquinho) and au (aumente). Reutilizável is divided re-u-ti-li-zá-vel, with the prefix re- (again) in a beat of its own. Ainda is a-ĩ-da: the n makes the i nasal, so ai is two beats here, not the diphthong of pai.

Many of the long words are built from a prefix and a suffix, and seeing the parts lets you read and spell them. Des- (not) + igual + -dade (-ity) gives desigualdade. In- (not) + evitar + -ável (able to be) gives inevitável. Re- + utilizar + -ável gives reutilizável. Sustentar + -ável + -idade gives sustentabilidade, where -ável becomes -abil- before -idade. The suffix -ção turns a verb into a noun (educar, educação; produzir, produção), and its plural is -ções. Recognizing the suffix also gives you the stress: words in -dade are stressed on da, and words in -ção on the suffix itself.

grammar.title: The whole system: moods, tenses and the question each one answers
grammar.explanation:
Two separate choices sit inside every Portuguese verb form. A tense places the action in time: before now, now or after now. A mood (the word means manner) shows the speaker's stance toward what the clause says. Portuguese has three moods. The indicative presents something as a fact, or as a belief the speaker holds to be true. The subjunctive presents something without asserting it: it is wished, doubted, feared, needed, conceded, imagined or still to come. The imperative gives commands. English keeps only traces of the subjunctive (if I were you, I suggest that he go), so English speakers lack the habit, which is why the Portuguese subjunctive feels hard. Portuguese uses it constantly, and the choice is not arbitrary. For every clause ask one question: is the speaker asserting this? If yes, the indicative. If no, the subjunctive, in the tense that fits the time.

The indicative tenses answer the question of when and how. The present states what is true now or habitually (estudo). The preterite reports a completed event (estudei), and the imperfect gives background, habit or an action in progress (estudava). The pluperfect, tinha estudado, places one past event before another past event. The future, estudarei or vou estudar, looks ahead. The conditional, estudaria, has three jobs that share one idea of distance from the present: it is the future seen from the past (ela disse que estudaria), the result of an imagined condition (se eu pudesse, estudaria) and the polite request (gostaria de). Learn these as answers to a question about time and attitude rather than as lists of endings. If you know what you want to say, the tense follows.

The subjunctive tenses work differently. They are not three meanings but three time slots, and the slot is chosen by the time of the main verb. The present subjunctive serves present and future triggers (Talvez ele venha; Quero que você venha). The imperfect subjunctive serves past triggers and imagined situations (Queria que você viesse; Se eu tivesse tempo, viajaria). The future subjunctive is used after se, quando, assim que, enquanto and similar words, and in relative clauses such as quem quiser, for events that have not happened yet (Quando você chegar, me avise). The perfect and pluperfect subjunctive, tenha feito and tivesse feito, place the event before the trigger (Duvido que ela tenha chegado; Esperava que ela tivesse chegado).

Conditions show the logic most clearly. Portuguese has three steps, as English does, but English climbs them by moving the indicative back in time (if it rains, if it rained, if it had rained), while Portuguese changes to subjunctive forms. A real possibility: Se chover, eu fico em casa (future subjunctive plus present). An imagined present or unlikely case: Se chovesse, eu ficaria em casa (imperfect subjunctive plus conditional). An impossible past: Se tivesse chovido, eu teria ficado em casa (pluperfect subjunctive plus conditional perfect, teria ficado). The further from reality, the more remote the forms. For possible or imagined conditions the if-clause takes the subjunctive, and for the imagined ones the result takes the conditional; never put the conditional in the if-clause. A condition treated as a fact takes the indicative (Se você diz isso, é verdade).

A fourth home for the subjunctive is the relative clause, which is a clause introduced by que or quem that describes a noun. If the speaker knows the noun exists and asserts it, the indicative is used: Conheço uma empresa que ajuda os funcionários. If the noun is wished for, sought, or not known to exist, the subjunctive is used: Procuro uma empresa que ajude os funcionários. The same logic explains uma tecnologia que sirva às pessoas in the first dialogue, where no such technology is claimed to exist yet. It also explains the set phrase há quem defenda, 'there are those who argue', where quem points to an unspecified group of people and the speaker does not say who.

The personal infinitive, which is the infinitive with person endings (entenderem, lucrarem, chegarmos), is the tool for an infinitive whose subject differs from the main verb: É importante eles entenderem o risco, Não basta lucrarem, Ao chegarmos. Finally, pronoun placement is a register choice. Register is the level of formality a situation calls for. In speech the pronoun goes before the verb (me avise, me disse); in formal writing it follows the verb at the start of a clause (avise-me, disse-me).

grammar.title: Concession: granting one fact and then contrasting it
grammar.explanation:
Concession means granting one fact and then saying something that pulls the other way: although it is late, I am staying. Its grammar rests on one idea that English speakers rarely meet. A conjunction is a word that joins two clauses, and the conjunction decides whether the two statements carry equal weight. Mas, porém and contudo join two full assertions of equal weight: É tarde, mas continuo. Embora, ainda que, mesmo que, por mais que and the formal conquanto make the first clause subordinate, meaning dependent on the main clause and placed in the background. The speaker grants it to the listener without putting weight on it, and Portuguese marks that stance with the subjunctive, even when the fact is certain. Embora seja tarde does not express doubt about the time; it means 'granted that it is late'. English although takes the ordinary indicative (although it is late), so this is one of the main differences between the two languages.

Por mais que works like 'however much' or 'no matter how much'. The mais is a comparison that can stretch as far as you like, so the clause concedes any degree of effort. Literally, por mais que eu tente is 'for more that I try'. The tense of the subjunctive follows the time. The present serves present and future (Por mais que eu estude, erro muito), the imperfect serves a past or imagined situation (Por mais que eu tentasse, não conseguia), the perfect serves something already completed (Por mais que tenha estudado, errou) and the pluperfect something completed before a past moment (Por mais que tivesse estudado, errou). The same tenses work after embora, ainda que and mesmo que. Mesmo que and ainda que cover both 'even if' and 'even though', which English separates, and the tense and context tell you which one is meant.

Apesar de is different in kind: it is a preposition, so it takes a noun, an adjective or an infinitive, not a conjugated clause: apesar da chuva, apesar de cansado, apesar de estar cansado. A preposition is a small word that links a noun or verb to what follows. When the subject changes, use the personal infinitive: apesar de eles estarem cansados. Apesar de que is also heard, but in careful writing use apesar de with an infinitive or embora. Historically apesar comes from a pesar de, in which pesar is a noun meaning regret or displeasure, so the phrase first meant 'to the displeasure of'.

Adversative connectors are the other half of the subject. An adversative connector is a word that opposes the sentence it begins to the sentence before it. These begin a new main clause and use the indicative: mesmo assim, ainda assim, apesar disso, no entanto, contudo, todavia, porém. Assim means thus and isso means that, and both point back at the previous statement, so mesmo assim is 'even so' and apesar disso is 'in spite of that'. The preposition de and the pronoun isso contract to disso, by the same rule as de plus a becoming da. Em contrapartida does something slightly different: it introduces a benefit or cost that balances the previous point, like a counterweight, and is translated 'on the other hand' or 'in return'. As for register, mas is the everyday word, porém and contudo belong more to writing, no entanto and todavia are formal, and mesmo assim, ainda assim and apesar disso work in speech and writing.

To choose, ask where the word sits. If a clause in the subjunctive follows it inside the sentence (por mais que, ainda que, embora, mesmo que), it is a conjunction. If it begins a fresh sentence or follows a semicolon (mesmo assim, apesar disso, no entanto), it is a connector and the indicative follows. Apesar de needs a noun, an adjective or an infinitive. The sentences Embora estivesse cansado, foi trabalhar and Estava cansado; mesmo assim, foi trabalhar say the same thing with two different structures.

grammar.title: Emphasis: cleft sentences and é que
grammar.explanation:
To emphasize a word, English usually raises the voice: JOHN solved it. Portuguese can also raise the voice, but it often restructures the sentence so that the important word is placed in a frame. The frame is called a cleft sentence, from the verb to cleave, because one clause is split into two parts. English has the same tool (It was John who solved it; What worries me is the future), and the Portuguese versions translate almost word for word.

The first frame is é or foi, then the highlighted element, then que, then the rest of the clause: Foi ela que resolveu o problema. The verb ser takes the tense of the event (foi for a completed event, é for a present or general one, era for past background) and comes before the highlighted word, which can be a subject, an object or an adverbial phrase. When the highlighted word is a person, quem can replace que: Foi ela quem resolveu. A preposition travels with the highlighted word: Foi com ela que falei, Foi em Salvador que nos conhecemos, É disso que eu falo. English can leave the preposition at the end (It was her I spoke with), but Portuguese cannot, so the preposition must stand in front of the emphasized phrase.

With a personal pronoun, the verb after que agrees with the pronoun: Fui eu que fiz, Fomos nós que decidimos. After quem the verb may also stay in the third person: Fui eu quem fez. Both are accepted. When the highlighted word is plural, ser usually agrees with it in careful usage: Foram eles que resolveram.

The second frame puts the highlighted element last. It begins with a relative clause, which is a clause that describes a noun, introduced by o que (the thing that) or quem (the person who), then ser, then the emphasized element: O que me preocupa é o futuro, Quem resolveu o problema foi ele. The relative clause acts as the subject, so the highlighted element is kept for the end, where the listener's attention is strongest. When the final element is plural, ser often agrees with it: O que me preocupa são os preços. The first frame can highlight almost any element, while the second works best for a subject or an object.

É que has three different jobs. After a question word it is an empty emphasizer that English has no equal for, mostly spoken: Onde é que você mora? means the same as Onde você mora? but sounds more engaged. At the start of a reply, É que introduces an explanation or an excuse: É que eu não sabia, 'it's just that I didn't know'. In the middle of a sentence it insists on who or what: Eu é que sei, 'I am the one who knows'.

Foi então que (it was then that), foi assim que (it was like that that) and foi por isso que (that is why) are the same frame with the highlight on time, manner and reason. They are the connective tissue of stories and arguments. In writing, use the frames sparingly, since each one adds words.

grammar.title: Common B2 errors and idiomatic usage
grammar.explanation:
Advanced learners do not make random errors. Most come from one of three sources: transferring an English structure, applying a pattern to a case it does not cover (for example, making a verb plural because the noun after it is plural), or confusing two forms that look alike. Each error below is explained by the rule it breaks, because a rule is easier to remember than a list of mistakes.

An impersonal verb is a verb with no subject at all, so it has no person and no number, and it stays in the third person singular whatever follows. Haver in its sense of 'to exist' is the main one (Há problemas, Houve problemas, Vai haver problemas), and fazer in time expressions is the other (Faz dois anos que moro aqui). The noun that follows is the object of haver, not its subject, which is why the verb does not agree with it. English says there were many problems and lets the verb follow the noun, so learners write houveram. An auxiliary verb (a helper such as dever, poder or ir) before an impersonal verb copies that behavior: Deve haver soluções, Pode haver problemas. Haver is historically the verb to have (from Latin habere), which is why há literally reads 'has'. In speech, tem replaces há (Tem muitos problemas), and that is natural.

After a preposition Portuguese uses special pronoun forms, mim and ti (para mim, entre mim e ti, sem ti), and the ordinary subject forms eu and tu are not used there. But mim is the form of a pronoun that is the object of the preposition. When the pronoun is the subject of an infinitive, it keeps the subject form, even though a preposition stands in front of the whole phrase: para eu fazer, sem eu saber. The test is whether the pronoun performs an action: if it does, it is a subject. Entre is a preposition whose two pronouns are both its objects, so entre mim e você is correct, and entre eu e você is an overcorrection by speakers who have learned to fear mim.

Regency (regência in Portuguese grammar books) is the preposition, or absence of one, that a verb requires. It is part of the verb's pattern and is not something you choose. English speakers import English patterns. Assistir a (to watch, as in assistir ao filme) requires the a in careful usage; everyday speech often says assistir o filme, and that is common, but formal writing keeps the a. Other verbs: preferir X a Y (prefiro café a chá), obedecer a (obedecer aos pais), discordar de and concordar com, sentir saudade de, arrepender-se de. With chegar, chegar à cidade is the formal choice and chegar na cidade is the spoken one.

Encontro means meeting or encounter. Ir ao encontro de is 'to go to meet', so you move toward something and welcome it: you agree with it or satisfy it. Ir de encontro a is 'to go against', so the two things collide. Only the small words change, which is why native speakers mix the pair up as well. A gente means we but is built from gente, a noun meaning people, so its verb takes the third person singular, as with any singular noun: a gente vai, a gente fez. The verb agrees with the grammar, not with the meaning. A gente vamos is heard in casual speech but marked as an error.

Two sets of look-alikes need separate treatment. Mas (but) and mais (more) differ by the i, which is a glide in the diphthong ai. Porque (one word, no accent) means because and answers a question. Por que (two words, no accent) asks why and also means 'for which' (Não sei por que ele saiu). Por quê, with the circumflex, is used at the end of a sentence (Você saiu por quê?), because quê is then a stressed one-syllable word ending in e, the exact case that takes a mark. O porquê, one word with the circumflex, is a noun meaning the reason (Ninguém sabe o porquê).

Gerundismo is the overuse of estar plus the gerund (the -ndo form, falando) to speak of the future: Vou estar enviando, Vamos estar verificando. It is a calque of English (I will be sending) spread by call-center scripts, and many speakers criticize it. The structure is not wrong in itself: Amanhã às dez eu vou estar trabalhando is fine, because it means I will be in the middle of working at ten. What is wrong is to use it when nothing is in progress and a simple verb would do: Vou enviar, Enviarei. A nível de is similarly criticized by purists when it means 'as regards'. Safer alternatives are em termos de, no âmbito de and quanto a. The form em nível de, meaning 'at the level of', is accepted.

grammar.title: Small words, constructions and register in the dialogues and readings
grammar.explanation:
The dialogues and readings of this unit contain short constructions that earlier units did not explain one by one. The table gives each with its literal meaning, because the literal meaning is the quickest way to see why it works, and then the natural meaning and the register. Register is the level of formality a situation calls for. The first dialogue is a formal debate: the moderator addresses the speakers as a senhora and o senhor, the pronoun follows the infinitive (usá-la, from usar plus a, with the r dropped and an acute on the new last syllable), and the phrases belong to written style (cabe a nós, não basta). The second dialogue is a chat among friends: cê, tá, tô, pra, né, cara and nossa, and the pronoun before the verb (me explicou, te empresto). Neither is more correct. Each is correct for its setting, and mixing them (tô in a formal debate, a senhora in a chat among friends) sounds out of place.

Several auxiliary verbs take a gerund, which is the verb form ending in -ndo, and mean something specific, which is why they are not gerundismo. Ir plus a gerund describes gradual progress (a gente vai se ajudando, 'we gradually help each other'). Viver plus a gerund describes something done again and again (vivo esquecendo, 'I keep forgetting'). Continuar plus a gerund means to go on (continua sendo importante). The preposition ao plus an infinitive means 'on doing' something: ao voltar is 'on returning', and ao longo de means 'over the course of'.

Quem can stand with no noun before it, and then it means 'the person who' or 'whoever': Quem viaja volta diferente. The same quem appears after a preposition: a quem sai, a quem volta e a quem fica, 'to those who leave, to those who come back and to those who stay'. The preposition stays in front of quem.

The impersonal se, met in the passive and impersonal unit, carries several expressions in the readings. Fala-se muito em sustentabilidade is 'there is a lot of talk about sustainability', and não se trata de means 'it is not a question of'. In each the verb has no specific subject, and the se marks that the doer is left unspecified.

culture.title: Como os brasileiros debatem
culture.text:
Debate in Brazil is often warm, expressive and overlapping. In an informal roda de conversa (literally 'wheel of conversation', a conversation circle) or at a mesa de bar ('bar table'), people interrupt each other as a sign of engagement, not rudeness, and arguing about football, politics and religion is a national pastime. Silence can mean disagreement more than politeness, so learners are encouraged to speak up.

In formal contexts the tone changes. Speakers soften disagreement with phrases such as com todo o respeito (literally 'with all the respect'), a meu ver ('at my to-see', in my view), não sei se concordo ('I don't know whether I agree') and pode ser, mas... ('it can be, but'), and they avoid saying 'you are wrong' directly. Talk shows, podcasts and the comment sections of news sites are a rich source of natural argument. The historian Sérgio Buarque de Holanda introduced the idea of the 'cordial man', and cordial comes from the Latin cor, heart: it means ruled by feeling and personal bonds rather than formal distance. The idea is often used to explain a mix of warmth and avoidance of open conflict, which is why a polite 'vamos ver' ('we-go to-see', let's see) can be a soft refusal.

For a learner moving beyond B2, the best investment is exposure to fast, spontaneous speech. Listen to interviews, radio debates and family conversations, where contractions like tá, pra, cê and vamo (vamos) are normal, and then compare them with the careful speech of newscasts and lectures. The unit's first dialogue and second dialogue show the two ends of that range. Being able to shift between these registers, and to argue a point without sounding either blunt or evasive, is the real mark of fluency.
